World.title: Two young boys kicked by stranger in Canberra shopping centre
World.content:
An 18-year-old man accused of assaulting two young boys at a Canberra shopping centre has been refused bail.

It is alleged the man approached the mother and the brothers, aged two and four, from behind, and kicked the children at Westfield Belconnen on Friday.

One of the boys was left with a broken nose while the other was assessed for head injuries.

Bystanders and centre security allegedly restrained the man for a time, but police did not respond to Triple Zero calls from the scene.

The man was arrested on Sunday, when he was charged with assault.

In a statement, police said they've apologised to the family for not attending the incident.

"The policing response to the incident was not in line with ACT Policing's expectations or the community's expectations," the statement said.

"We want to reassure the ACT community this is not our standard response protocol and ACT Policing is reviewing the policing response to this incident."

Bail refused amid 'a dangerous and volatile situation'

The man appeared in the ACT Magistrates Court this morning visibly distressed after a night in custody, with his lawyer telling the court he had significant mental impairments.

In seeking bail, the man's lawyer argued his NDIS supports would be suspended if he was remanded in custody, and conditions could be imposed to deal with any risk of reoffending.

But prosecutor Marcus Dyason told the court the man had a fixation on young children.

"The accused targets those who cannot protect themselves," Mr Dyason said.

"Releasing the accused on bail with a hope — and it is a hope — is of little comfort to the community.

"There are no conditions that could be imposed … that could ameliorate the risks to an acceptable level."

The 18-year-old accused has been refused bail in the ACT Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Chief Magistrate Louise Taylor described the alleged behaviour as "dangerous, impulsive and frightening", and questioned why he'd been allowed to be at the shopping centre without supervision.

"It's a very dangerous and volatile situation that's been created," she said.

"There's a fixation on little people which only elevates the risk he poses.

"I cannot fathom a decision that allowed him to be alone in the community.

"I can't control the behaviour of others around him and bail conditions can only control [his] conduct."

The man's lawyer said inquiries were underway as to whether his current level of one-to-one supervision could be raised to 24 hours a day.

But Magistrate Taylor agreed the man posed a risk to vulnerable members of the community, and said the jail had a duty of care to provide the required supports while in custody.

She also ordered the man's name not be published.

Mother: 'Police didn't bother sending a patrol'

In a social media post following the incident, the boys' mother shared that ACT Police did not respond to "multiple triple-0 calls" for help.

"The offender was restrained at the time by members of the public and Westfield security, but ACT police didn't bother sending a patrol," the mother wrote on Saturday.

Police say two Triple Zero calls about the incident were made at the time but officers didn't attend. (ABC News)

She said she followed up with police multiple times in-person and over the phone "to find out when someone will be in contact with me to help, and no one can provide much info".

"No one from ACT police has spoken to me about what occurred or checked if my boys are ok," she wrote.

Police have since confirmed that two Triple Zero calls about the incident were made at the time, and that officers did not attend.

ACT Deputy Chief Police Officer Richard Chin told ABC Canberra Breakfast police "didn't get it right".

"Our response to the family at that time and after the incident wasn't in line with our own expectations as ACT Policing and it certainly wasn't in line with what the community would expect from us," he said.

Assistant Commissioner Chin said police have since met with the family.

"When we realised our response wasn't up to scratch, we met with and apologised unreservedly to the family involved," he said.

"We absolutely should have done better."

Assistant Commissioner Chin says police didn't prioritise the incident appropriately. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine )

Minister questions why higher priority wasn't given

Assistant Commissioner Chin said ACT Policing was reviewing its response to the incident.

"We want to really look into this to understand what happened," he said.

"But clearly there was a breakdown in understanding the urgency of the response that we need to provide during this incident and also afterwards to the family concerned.

" We simply didn't prioritise this matter appropriately, and I really apologise for that to the family. "

ACT Police Minister Marisa Paterson told ABC Canberra Breakfast she was "shocked" by the police response.

"I couldn't understand why there hadn't been a police response to this incident," she said.

"An incident like this would be considered by everyone to be very high priority.

"And so the questions around why it wasn't prioritised at the level it should have been is very important that we do get answers to this.

"We need to understand why this has happened to ensure that it won't happen again."

Marisa Paterson says Canberrans should have have confidence in calling Triple Zero. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Dr Paterson said the situation shouldn't have happened and she assured Canberrans they could continue to have confidence in calling Triple Zero.

"I do want to reiterate that this was a very serious incident that should have had a high priority response, and if you do call Triple Zero in the case of an emergency, police will respond," she said.

The 18-year-old man's case is expected to return to court next month.

World.title: Coles and Woolworths test facial recognition technology
World.content:
Coles and Woolworths have conducted tests of facial recognition technology, but it is unclear if either supermarket will be implementing it in stores.

It comes after the Australia Financial Review reported both Coles and Woolworths had trialled the technology as part of an ongoing effort to combat retail crime.

The article said both supermarket giants had "conducted early testing" of the technology.

When the ABC asked Coles about the potential of it being rolled out in stores, a spokesperson made a distinction between the use of the term "test" instead of "trial".

"Coles has not done a trial using this technology," the spokesperson said.

"A small, one-off, controlled proof-of-concept test of the technology was undertaken which did not use customer or team member information or data.

"No decision has been made about the deployment of facial recognition technology."

AI facial recognition technology has been subject to debate over privacy concerns. (Four Corners: Nick Wiggins)

The spokesperson said Coles did not currently use facial recognition technology in stores.

The ABC understands Woolworths tested the technology in its New Zealand office.

A Woolworths spokesperson did not address the ABC's questions on how facial recognition technology was tested or if it would be used in Australia.

"Keeping our team and customers safe is the most important thing we do and we've put significant investment towards this," the spokesperson said.

"While our current safety initiatives are making a difference, we are still seeing a concerning amount of aggression and conflict incidents in our stores on a daily basis, including weapons being presented."

Police facial recognition trial More than 130,000 faces have already been scanned under WA Police's landmark facial recognition trial. The privacy watchdog, experts and Aboriginal advocates are raising concerns about who could be caught in its net.

Facial recognition technology has been subject to debate over privacy concerns and misidentification with particular demographic groups.

Bunnings wins fight to use AI facial recognition

In February, Australian hardware giant Bunnings won a legal battle to monitor its customers with AI.

Bunnings had breached privacy laws by scanning hundreds of thousands of customers' faces without their proper consent, the privacy commissioner found in 2024.

The Administrative Review Tribunal found that facial recognition technology could be used in limited circumstances to address retail crime and protect staff and customers from violence and abuse.

Bunnings wins fight to use AI facial recognition tech Bunnings was reasonably entitled to use the technology to combat crime and staff abuse, the Administrative Review Tribunal finds.

The decision could provide a legal framework for other retailers to follow Bunnings in embracing the use of AI to reduce the risk of crime in their stores.

Retailers spruik tech for 'modern safety challenges'

The Australian Retail Council (ARC) represents small, medium and large retail businesses across Australia.

Chief executive Chris Rodwell said retail workers were facing "unacceptable levels of violence, threats, intimidation and abuse in stores".

"Used responsibly and in the right context, technology can play an important role in tackling modern safety challenges," Mr Rodwell said.

"Facial recognition can help retailers identify known high-harm repeat offenders when they enter a store, allowing staff to take appropriate action before another violent or threatening incident occurs.

The Privacy Commissioner has published updated guidance on the technology. (Supplied: Woolworths Group)

"The industry is committed to getting this right for workers, customers and the community.

"That's why retailers are taking the time to test its use and ensure its rollout is aligned with the Privacy Commissioner's guidelines and community expectations."

In July, the Privacy Commissioner published updated guidance allowing facial recognition to be used in public spaces, including retail stores.

How common is supermarket crime?

A survey from the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association (SDA), the union for retail, fast food and warehouse workers, found about a third of workers did not feel safe in their workplace.

The SDA's most recent data, which was published at the end of last year, was based on a survey of nearly 3,000 workers.

It found that, over the period of 12 months:

34 per cent of members said they did not feel safe in their workplace

88 per cent experienced verbal abuse

25 per cent experienced physical violence

19 per cent experienced sexual harassment

11 per cent experienced online abuse

10 per cent had been spat on

31 per cent experienced ethnicity/race/cultural background-related abuse or harassment

59 per cent had been abused by the same customer more than once

Both Coles and Woolworths said they would continue to investigate initiatives to ensure worker and customer safety.

World.title: Anthony Albanese's teen social media ban has a shark problem
World.content:
Years into Australia's quest to get teens off social media, the Albanese government is suddenly in a hurry.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last month declared it was "outrageous" that the Coalition and the Greens had voted to scrutinise proposed reforms to social media minimum age law at an inquiry.

It was oddly urgent for a policy that had been in the works for more than two years — and one that he declared a "success" a week before it even came into effect.

Now, eight months after the law was implemented, there is a clearer explanation for the government's haste: its world-first policy for Australians aged under 16 has so far produced little visible change.

Anthony Albanese says it is "outrageous" Coalition and the Greens voted to scrutinise proposed reforms. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Early teen social media ban results show little impact

Late last month, the government's independent online safety regulator, eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant, released the first findings of its expert-led study of the ban's results.

The top line was that use of social media by teens had barely budged. Most teens (81.5 per cent) were still using social media after the ban, down just a few percentage points from 85.9 per cent before the ban.

(It also reported a 20 per cent decrease in teens with accounts on social media, although the ban's law, as written, actually doesn't require social media companies to stop teens from using social media in a logged-out state).

Age-check providers want social giants tested In a damning submission, an age-check firm warns big fines may be seen as a "small price to pay" if copping them allows Australia's ban to be "wrongly" be portrayed as a failure.

It found little change to kids' offline activities, problematic internet use or wellbeing, nor to parental stress.

A bigger impact found by the research was that parents are now increasingly in the dark about their teens' social media use, with those who were unaware their teens had used social media going from 23 per cent to 33 per cent.

Then, at the inquiry into the ban's amendments on Friday, the eSafety Commissioner acknowledged that the office had also seen a rise in messaging and gaming use — two exclusions from the teen social media ban that, nevertheless, undercut the government's promise to get kids "back onto the footy field".

Now, this is just a policy that's only been in effect for a few months. Online child safety group SmackTalk's founder Wayne Holesworth told the hearing that it would take three to five years for the ban's effects to be fully felt.

But it's still remarkable that, eight months after coming into effect, the most positive case for Albanese's globally celebrated teen social media ban is: Well, we haven't actually done it properly yet so it still might work out.

There were warnings

It's easy to say that we couldn't have known how this world-first ban would play out.

But if you look back at the public submissions made before the ban was legislated, back in November 2024, some experts and groups concerned about the ban seemed to have a good idea.

The Australian Human Rights Commission warned that technological workarounds would undermine the success of the ban.

The Australian Research Alliance for Children and Youth said that bans would drive young people to other places.

Academics Marcus Carter, Taylor Hardwick and Ben Egliston said that they believed children's social media use would become "more private, and more hidden".

One particularly prescient submission warned that age restriction efforts on platforms were already ineffective in practice and that bans by themselves would not teach young people to use the internet more safely.

That was a submission from the eSafety Commissioner, the regulator who's now been tasked with enforcing this law.

Some experts and groups have been concerned about the efficacy of the ban. (Reuters: Asanka Brendon)

Who's to blame?

The government has been quick to blame social media companies for failing to enforce the ban and, by extension, its political opponents for any delay on new powers to help enforce it.

What the teen social media ban actually did was require tech companies to take "reasonable steps" to keep teens off their platform.

The fact that teens are still on these platforms is not proof that the companies haven't followed the law as written. (Inman Grant says investigations into five social media platforms are ongoing.)

In fact, the government made it clear that it didn't want the social media companies to be too strict on enforcing the law. It literally wrote into law that companies couldn't only ask for ID, and had to give the option of other, less accurate methods. Its porousness is by design.

Why are so many under-16s still on social media? Research suggests many under-16s are still active on social media platforms. BTN High explores why and tests the accuracy of popular technology used to estimate age.

This all makes the government's proposed fix to the ban to double the size of the fines seem ridiculous — maybe it should first use the stick before seeing if there's a bigger one.

But let's assume that the tech companies have broken the law. Why is the government surprised?

After all, it has pilloried the companies, accused them of not caring and of causing social harm — calling them "sharks".

It has a lot of good reasons to do that. Look no further than the US courts finding that companies like Meta are a "public nuisance" causing psychological harm and sexual exploitation, or whistleblower files revealing that the company buried research showing the deleterious impacts of its products on teen mental health.

These are companies that evidently can't be left to self-regulate. And yet, the government wrote the ban in a way that left the details of enforcement to the companies it said couldn't be trusted.

To continue the government's own metaphor, it's like it let the sharks design the shark nets.

Now, it says those companies aren't complying and it needs new powers to prove it.

Which prompts the question: why wasn't the law designed with those powers in the first place? Didn't you say we were dealing with sharks?

Loading

The road not taken

Too often, Australia's teen social media ban is evaluated on an all-or-nothing basis: if not the ban, we would've just been sitting around, twiddling our thumbs.

But there other options which demonstrate the real opportunity cost pursuing the ban — look no further than the government's other online safety policy.

Since November 2024, the Albanese government says it is planning to introduce a digital duty of care, a new policy that would give tech companies a broad obligation to mitigate and reduce harms from using their services.

Nearly two years later, that's yet to be brought before parliament. We may be years away from it kicking in.

What of the road not taken? What if instead of years spent developing the policy, promoting it publicly, taking it to the UN, now being tied up in legal battles, Australia had gone full throttle with the digital duty of care?

We can't know for sure but it seems common sense that the ban has taken up oxygen and resources that could have been used elsewhere.

Which brings us back around to the stakes of this whole issue: helping young people.

The reason the ban has and continues to be such a popular idea is that Australians are worried about our teens.

It's that energy that justifies spending more time on the teen social media ban to see if we can make it work. It's not surprising that a world-first ban isn't perfect out of the gate.

But at some point, that same desire to improve the lives of young people means that the government may want to consider its commitment and investment in a policy that's yet to show any results.

It's hard to imagine another high-profile policy involving something as important as our children suffering such obvious early setbacks and not prompting more discussion about whether it's something that we should be single-mindedly pursuing.

If Albanese is right and there's no time to waste, how much more of it can we spend just waiting for the ban to work?

World.title: US star Hayden Panettiere dies aged 36
World.content:
American actor Hayden Panettiere has died at the age of 36, according to reports by US media.

She was best known for TV shows such as Nashville and Heroes.

In a statement provided to US outlet ABC News, Panettiere's father, Skip, said his daughter was "a force of nature".

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden," he said.

"She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her, and to the millions who watched her on-screen".

No cause of death was announced, and a publicist for the actor did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press.

Hayden Panettiere at the 21st Annual Critics' Choice Awards in 2016. (Reuters: Danny Moloshok)

Panettiere had a prolific career dating back to 1996, and her credits included the voice of Dot in A Bug's Life, Remember the Titans and Scream VI.

Her role as a cheerleader with superpowers in Heroes propelled her to fame, with the series revolving around the mantra, "Save the cheerleader, save the world".

In Nashville, she starred as fictional country singer Juliette Barnes. The musical drama series ran from 2012 to 2018.

Panettiere sang all of her character's own songs, and her performance earned her two Golden Globe nominations for best supporting actress in 2013 and 2014.

She had been open about her struggles with alcohol addiction and depression, including after the birth of her daughter in 2014.

In a memoir published this year, titled This Is Me: A Reckoning, she wrote about her decision to give full custody of her daughter to her former partner, boxer Wladimir Klitschko.

ABC/wires

World.title: Kangaroo Island community 'desperately cranky' as ferries delayed again
World.content:
Kangaroo Island's long-awaited new ferry service will be delayed again, more than 12 months after it was supposed to start.

The two new vehicles, delivered by SeaLink, were initially expected to begin service early last year, but last October the company adjusted the commencement to June 1 this year.

In April, transport minister Joe Szakacs said the ferries would not be ready by June, and the following month SeaLink confirmed that delay and said the service would commence "on or before 23 September 2026".

Electrical components on Ruwi were damaged in final testing of fire deluge systems, delaying the vessel's delivery to South Australia. (Supplied: SeaLink)

SeaLink has now revised the start date to November, citing an "incident" during the final testing of its second vessel, Ruwi, which remains in Indonesia where it was built.

Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly said he and the community were "desperately cranky" at the situation.

"[The community has] sort of been misled for a long time and haven't had straight answers, and for this to happen now at the eleventh hour is really quite distressing to many people," he said.

In October last year, SeaLink said the first ferry — Wanggami — would be arriving "late 2025". That vessel reached Port Adelaide in April this year.

In its May announcement, SeaLink said Ruwi was expected to reach Port Adelaide "by August".

It has now revised that to "late September", following an incident during the harbour commissioning and final testing process.

Michael Pengilly says the community is "desperately cranky" at the situation. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

"The shipbuilder undertook a fire deluge test and unfortunately a temporary pipe that was used for testing purposes failed, which resulted in discharge of water which discharged onto electrical components," acting chief operating officer for SeaLink, Phil Boyle, said.

"The affected electrical components have been replaced, but unfortunately what that has done has delayed the arrival of Ruwi, the second new vessel, into South Australia by about three weeks."

The transport minister said he was "very concerned" by the latest update.

"In fact, I'm angry," Joe Szakacs said.

Ferry whiplash

Mr Pengilly said the repeated delays and lack of certainty were having an impact on the island and its tourists.

"Kangaroo Islanders are sick of being told when the boat is starting, then it's not starting, then it's starting again," he said.

"Really, what we want to see is some straight answers and some humble pie from SeaLink.

"And potentially, some compensation for people who are losing a considerable amount of money."

He said the island community was "quite decidedly cynical" about the new service.

"It's just disappointing that it's got to this, so it's been changed yet again, and it leaves us up in the air about capacity to get on the ferry.

"It's really disturbing regarding livestock movement at the busiest time of the year."

The first new ferry, Wanggami, was officially christened on July 30. (Supplied: SeaLink)

Mr Boyle said SeaLink "had a choice to make" when it became clear Ruwi would not arrive in time for the planned three-day shutdown from September 1.

"Either proceed with the shutdown and expose Kangaroo Island to an extended period of reduced capacity and reliability, or postpone the works for a short while and maintain the existing ferry," he said.

"This is an essential service for the community. So postponing the works that was planned for the first to the fourth of September was the most responsible decision.

"We're not prepared to introduce an added risk to its reliability just to meet that September date."

Michael Esposito, who manages his family's olive business on Kangaroo Island, said the latest delay would have a "very minimal" impact.

Michael Esposito says the most recent delay was out of SeaLink's control. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

"Given the fact we've got two existing ferries currently still in operation, I can't see how the delay will materially affect day-to-day operations in our business," he said.

"There's only so much that SeaLink can control, and given the most recent delay has been something outside of their control, as frustrating as it is, I think it's more important to get it right.

" I think there would be a lot more unhappy people if the infrastructure works and the transition wasn't done to the highest possible standard and as smooth as possible. "

A communication breakdown

Throughout the project, SeaLink's communication has been repeatedly criticised.

Kangaroo Island ferries delayed Two new SeaLink ferries for Kangaroo Island, which were initially expected to begin service in early 2025, then pushed back to June this year, have been delayed for a second time.

In April, Mr Pengilly said SeaLink's communication had been "pathetically inadequate".

Today, Mr Szakacs said he was "incredibly disappointed with the communication from SeaLink".

"I was made aware of this [delay] very, very late last week by SeaLink," the minister told 891 ABC Adelaide.

Late last month, SeaLink South Australia general manager Tracey Croft told 891 ABC Adelaide Drive there were limitations on what it could say due to a government contract.

"We have some limitations about speaking freely," she said.

Joe Szakacs says he has been "disappointed" in the communications from SeaLink. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"Most commentary has to be approved by the state government before we are allowed to release media statements."

Asked about this today, Mr Szakacs said no such limitations existed.

Asked if he was concerned SeaLink was throwing him under the bus, the minister said he was.

"Absolutely, I've expressed this to them personally … It was a good conversation, and I think there's no confusion now," Mr Szakacs said.

World.title: Ray Hadley and Peter FitzSimons told about Alan Jones claims, court hears
World.content:
A former colleague of Alan Jones has told a court he confided in broadcaster Ray Hadley and author Peter FitzSimons that Mr Jones had allegedly kissed and touched him at work, but declined to go public with the accusations and asked Mr Hadley not to report it.

Complainant C is giving a second day of evidence in Mr Jones's indecent assault and sexual touching trial in the NSW Local Court, where he has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges.

The man told the trial last week that Mr Jones kissed him without consent several times in the lift of his Circular Quay apartment and at work, and touched his crotch in the car while he was driving the radio host.

The man, who was in his early 20s when the alleged offending began, told the court today Mr Hadley asked in 2019 if he would like to speak to author and former rugby union player Peter FitzSimons, because he was researching allegations about Mr Jones.

Ray Hadley was a long-time broadcast rival of Alan Jones. (AAP)

The complainant said he was with Mr Hadley when Mr FitzSimons called the broadcaster, and he agreed to speak to the author on the phone, but declined to go on the record.

"I told him how Alan used to kiss me, how he used to touch me on the penis," Complainant C said.

"How it happened when I was driving him.

"Peter asked me if I wanted to tell that story publicly and I immediately declined.

"At no point did I tell him who I was, at no point did I identify myself."

He said he had never previously disclosed the allegations to Mr Hadley, who sat and listened to the phone conversation.

Peter FitzSimons was researching allegations against Alan Jones. (ABC/Wooden Horse/WildBear Entertainment/Artemis Media)

"Ray asked if I was OK … I just broke down sobbing," he said. "And I said he's a f***ing grub. "I said he's a f***ing c***. "He offered to go with me to the police. "And I said, 'No, I don't want to do anything like that'. "I asked him to give me an assurance he wouldn't tell anyone."

Accuser refused to go public

Asked why he refused to tell the story publicly, Complainant C said at that point he did not want people to know what had happened, and said he was aware Mr FitzSimons did not like Mr Jones.

"I didn't want to be associated with anything like that," he said.

Complainant C said he confided in four friends and two colleagues about Mr Jones's alleged offending before that conversation with Mr Hadley, including telling one person that the radio host was a "grub" and that he "used to grab me on the c***".

But Complainant C also described an unwillingness to let people know about the alleged offending.

In 2013, when he was no longer working with Mr Jones, he said he was still receiving and responding to "romantic, intimate messages" from the defendant.

Asked why he continued to respond, he said it was important professionally to continue a good relationship with Mr Jones.

"These things had happened with Alan and I didn't want anyone to know," he said. "So, in many ways I wanted to keep on his side."

He admitted inviting Mr Jones to his wedding after a discussion with his wife, telling the court, "I felt I needed to."

He said in 2014 he worked for a politician, and told the court he was asked about his relationship with Mr Jones in the job interview.

Complainant C described the talkback host as "very, very important to state politics" at the time, and that "often, policy was decided by some of the topics Alan was working on".

Text messages relayed in court

The court heard that in 2023, Complainant C agreed to meet with Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) investigative journalist Kate McClymont after she contacted him.

He said he spoke to her about his experiences with Mr Jones, but did not authorise her to use his name.

The SMH published an article about Mr Jones in December that year, and the complainant told the court that to his knowledge, he had never met or spoken to any of the people who were making allegations in the story.

Complainant C was also taken through a collection of text messages between himself and Mr Jones.

In several messages, Mr Jones made reference to the size of Complainant C's penis, including in one message from 2014, and the complainant replied that seeing Mr Jones again that day was "the highlight of my day".

He told the court he deliberately did not respond to references to his genitals.

Complainant C said when Mr Jones referenced his genitals in a message, he would attempt to "defuse that sort of message".

"It's deeply embarrassing to read, but it's also deeply embarrassing to receive, because I didn't feel that way," he said.

"I would send those messages because it is how I felt I had to engage."

Alan Jones has denied all the allegations. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

In another message, Complainant C spoke about a job offer from the politician and said, "can't sleep, thinking of you tonight".

"That was how you had to text him," Complainant C told the court. "There was a routine to it. You had to text him in a flirty way." "Why is that?" Crown prosecutor Georgina Wright SC asked. "To curry favour. As I said, and I'll say it again, I hate reading these messages," he replied.

In June 2014, Mr Jones texted C "I love you intensely", and in October that year, the broadcaster referenced that he "would love big hugs and kisses with you".

The court heard in October 2014, Mr Jones sent a message which Complainant C interpreted as a request for a picture of his genitals.

"I didn't respond," he told the court.

In 2015, Complainant C sent Mr Jones a message saying "love you mate" and "always thinking of you", while referencing something Mr Jones had said on air that morning.

Asked why he included the "thinking of you" phrase, he told the court: "That was how I engaged with him."

Complainant confided in father-in-law

Complainant C said he also confided in his father-in-law about the broadcaster's alleged offending during a discussion about the #MeToo movement, and the sexual abuse claims being made against Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein.

"I recall [my father-in-law] making a comment about people coming forward making claims against high profile people for money … just to make a name for themselves," he said.

"I said, 'Well now is probably a good time to tell you, this is what Alan Jones did to me, and it's responses like that that would stop me from saying what happened'.

"I'm now the father of your grandchild and I wouldn't want my name out there."

He said his father-in-law then apologised and expressed sympathy.

The witness was also asked about another alleged kiss in Melbourne, which is not the subject of a charge, but was allowed to be introduced as "context or relationship" evidence.

He gave evidence that Mr Jones kissed him at the Crown Melbourne hotel in 2012, when he was invited by another man to visit the defendant after an AFL game.

Complainant C said Mr Jones had asked him alone to come on a "tour" of the hotel room, and approached him immediately after they entered the walk-in wardrobe.

The witness said he raised both hands and pushed the defendant away, and the pair rejoined others in the main area of the apartment.

World.title: Sydney Swans CEO confirms police investigating alleged incident 'involving several players'
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have confirmed several of their footballers were involved in an "alleged incident" in Melbourne last night.

The Swans issued a statement just after midday today.

"The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage," the club said.

Victoria Police separately issued a statement saying detectives were investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne.

The Sydney Swans stayed at the Pullman in East Melbourne last night. (ABC News)

"The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning," a spokesperson said.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing."

Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich called a press conference this afternoon that lasted less than one minute.

"We're still piecing together exactly what's transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing," he said.

"Safe to say, we're extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation.

"We understand the level of interest in the matter and there's going to be lots of speculation, but given it's a police matter right now, that's all that we can say."

Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich addressed the media this afternoon. (ABC News)

The Swans were staying in Melbourne overnight after their 36-point win over Essendon at the MCG yesterday.

Sydney is sitting in second spot on the AFL ladder heading into the final round of the 2026 season, with the finals due to start within weeks.

The team has had 17 wins this season and is due to play its next game at home at the SCG against North Melbourne.

World.title: ABC removes more episodes by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal
World.content:
The ABC has withdrawn a further two episodes by sacked Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal and edited another due to concerns about anonymous interviewees.

Fazal's employment was terminated in May after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year, ABC managing director Hugh Marks confirmed at a Senate estimates hearing in May.

Since then, two episodes he reported for Four Corners, titled Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway, have been removed by the ABC due to accuracy concerns. A Background Briefing audio program he reported, titled Remy was 12 when she became a drug dealer, was also removed later in July.

In a statement, the ABC said it had completed a review of anonymous interviewees in all stories reported by Fazal for the two programs, which identified concerns with three more programs.

"The review found that in each of these cases, ABC verification policies concerning the use of anonymous interviewees were not followed to a level that meets our editorial standards," the statement said.

"Therefore, in order to ensure complete confidence in published content, we have taken the decision to remove them."

'Cocaine dealer' on Fazal's Four Corners episode says she played 'an acting role' Further concerns over the accuracy of reporting by sacked Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal are raised on Media Watch, including that a hire car was used to mislead viewers in the profile of a purported cocaine dealer.

Two stories — Four Corners episode Silent Orders and Background Briefing episode Meet the teens at the frontline of organised crime — have been removed from ABC platforms.

A short segment contributed by Fazal in the Four Corners episode The Postcode Wars, in which he says he visits a drug "trap house", has been edited out.

"Outside of this segment the episode meets our editorial standards and will remain available online with an editor's note," the statement said.

"The ABC is committed to journalism of the highest standard. Maintaining the trust of Australians depends on upholding those standards and we take any concerns about our journalism seriously."

From Mongols bikie to award-winning reporter

Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, is an award-winning journalist specialising in reporting on crime, violence, imprisonment and terrorism.

His reporting has appeared in VICE, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.

After the Four Corners episodes were removed, Fazal said in a statement posted to social media that he was "shocked" by the decision.

"I believe the process ABC is following and its decisions so far set a worrying precedent for the organisation's independent [sic] and commitment to public-interest journalism," he said.

Fazal claimed in another video statement he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources, with that proximity later used against him.

He said his reporting was heavily scrutinised during editorial standards and production meetings.

Fazal has been contacted for further comment in light of the additional removal of episodes.

Earlier this month, the ABC announced its head of investigations and current affairs, Jo Puccini, was leaving the public broadcaster after a 25-year career.

She had oversight of Four Corners and Background Briefing.

Other senior managers at the ABC at the time of Fazal's reporting have already left the broadcaster.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination of ‘complainant C’  begins after court told Jones offered man tour of Packer suite before kissing him in walk-in wardrobe
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day nine of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleague Clare Sibthorpe will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear further evidence today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Monday. KATE GERAGHTY

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Jones is charged with indecently assaulting “C” eight times over a five-month period by touching and kissing him without his consent.

“C” told the court on Friday that Jones bombarded him with “love-bombing” in text messages before the alleged incidents started.

He said he told Jones “no” repeatedly before the then 2GB host kissed him for the first time in the lift of the broadcaster’s harbourside apartment, but the “extraordinary” power imbalance stopped him speaking out as the alleged assaults continued.

He also told the court that Jones touched him under the table on the penis over his clothing at a lunch in Sydney in front of other guests. He said one guest asked him after the lunch if he had “copped a feel”, a remark that left him “deeply embarrassed”.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Forrestania inks $27M mining deal for Tycho gold mine in WA goldfields
World.content:
Forrestania Resources has taken a major stride in its transition from explorer to producer, awarding a $27 million open pit mining contract for its Tycho gold project near Coolgardie in Western Australia to MEGA Resources. The contract award is a critical milestone and puts the company on a clear path towards its first gold pour.

The move comes against a backdrop of feverish activity in the Australian gold sector. With gold prices still stubbornly strong after hitting record highs earlier in the year, WA’s goldfields are a hotbed of corporate activity and consolidation. The buoyant market is keeping mining service providers busy, with contractors being locked in across the state as producers look to capitalise on the high-price environment.

MEGA Resources’ fleet of Cat 777 dump trucks may soon see service on Forrestania Resources Tycho open pit mining operation in WA.

The new contract covers a stage one open pit mining campaign at Tycho and includes drill and blast, mining, haulage and ore delivery services over an approximate seven-month duration. World.title: Trump’s shocking grab for power will create secrecy for him and his cronies
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Opinion Trump’s shocking grab for power will create secrecy for him and his cronies Noah Feldman Law professor and columnist August 17, 2026 — 2:30pm

August 17, 2026 — 2:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump administration’s latest assertions about executive privilege — that it protects the confidentiality of a president’s communication with private advisers who aren’t part of the government — are like too much else in this White House: politically unprecedented, legally wrong and morally dubious. From a legal standpoint, the point of executive privilege is to protect communications that occur within the government, between the president and other public officials. Politically speaking, this is a naked attempt to protect the president from congressional investigation of potentially corrupt deals with his cronies, any of whom who could be called “advisers” to avoid subpoena. President Donald Trump gestures as he boards Air Force One on Sunday. AP If President Donald Trump invokes this executive privilege in future fights with Congress, as seems likely, the legislative branch cannot fold. It must insist on its rights, bring the issue to court, and force the Supreme Court to reject the claim. The Trump administration’s claims come in the form of a new memo by the assistant attorney general in charge of the Office of Legal Counsel, known as OLC. Historically, OLC has tended to adopt a maximalist position on presidential power. At the same time, the office has traditionally worked to maintain legitimacy by sticking to its independent understanding of the scope of presidential authority. That is supposed to mean not knuckling under to White House pressure except in rare (and infamous) cases, such as the so-called torture memos written and subsequently withdrawn by OLC lawyers under President George W. Bush.



As this memo demonstrates, Trump’s OLC has no qualms about giving the president exactly what he wants. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump has been humbled over his pet project. This obsession hurts him, even when he’s right Cory Alpert Former White House staffer But the doctrine of executive privilege has never been extended to conversations between the president and people who were not part of the government. The memo claims support from a 2007 OLC memo signed by then-acting attorney general Paul Clement. That memo suggests that executive privilege could extend to government officials outside the executive branch, which is a debatable point that the courts have not addressed. At any rate, that memo was specifically referring to conversations between the president and members of the Senate who would play a role in confirming US attorneys. That comes nowhere near the claim that the president should just be able to apply the privilege to conversations with private citizens. Nor does the Trump memo have any convincing arguments why it should. It says that some experts are not in the government and the president should be able to get their unvarnished opinions. But a modern government should include experts capable of advising the president on every important topic. If the best experts are on the outside and the president wants their confidential advice, he can always bring them in, the way he brought in various Department of Government Efficiency advisers from the private sector at the beginning of his second term. Once they are official White House employees, their communications with the president would be privileged. One of the most shocking parts of the memo is its assertion that private advisers without guaranteed confidentiality might be constrained in what they would say to the president because of “concern about appearances”. As OLC seems not to realise, that concern nicely captures the madness of this assertion of executive privilege: It is essentially saying that the president and his cronies should be able to make all kinds of corrupt deals or bargains, whether illegal or just immoral, without worrying about them being disclosed.



Put another way: When people who don’t work for the government talk to the president, it is entirely appropriate — desirable, even — for them to be concerned about appearances. More than any other administration in recent history, Trump operates on the basis of personalised relationships. He doesn’t just call executives of major companies to get advice. He calls to bully them into doing what he wants. No doubt he also receives calls from people seeking favours. In both cases, these kinds of communications should not be protected by privilege under the guise of advice-to the president. Loading Consider why executive privilege exists in the first place. The core idea is that the president should be able to get the advice he needs to run the government from the people who are best suited to provide it. Those people are government officials, who take an oath to uphold the Constitution and follow the laws. They are subject to all kinds of conflict-of-interest rules designed to make sure their advice is based on the national interest.



What’s more, the identities of White House advisers are public. That’s because in a democracy, the public is entitled to know who is advising the president — and to be sure that they are serving the nation’s interests, not their own. In the White House, the president can hire and fire the advisers he wants. They don’t have to be confirmed by the Senate. They do, however, have to be loyal to the government elected by the people. For their communications with the president to be protected by executive privilege, the adviser should have to be fully committed to their public role. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s great humiliation: Middle East may be entering a post-American era Peter Hartcher Political and international editor There are other problems with the memo. For example, it repeats the traditional rule that privilege extends to “communications solicited and received by the President or his direct advisers.” But it would clearly be crazy to apply that rule when White House officials who are not the president consult private parties on policy. That would expand what’s already an outrageous claim of privilege for the president into an even more outrageous privilege for many White House officials when they are speaking to private parties. What’s more, the memo doesn’t say whether the “direct advisers” covered by the privilege would now include private non-governmental advisers. If it did, then the consequences would be perverse. A CEO, for example, could claim adviser privilege in a document he or his staff created, in anticipation of speaking to the president — with the result that executive privilege could extend well into corporate America.



The biggest problem, though, is the obvious one. Donald Trump, the most corrupt president of the modern age, is asserting a broad new executive privilege designed to protect precisely corrupt cronyism. Neither Congress nor the courts can let that become the law. Noah Feldman is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist and a professor of law at Harvard University. He is an author, most recently, of To Be a Jew Today: A New Guide to God, Israel, and the Jewish People. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Shocked and disappointed’: Swans boss speaks as players investigated over alleged sexual assault
World.content:
Sydney chief executive Matthew Pavlich says the club is “shocked and disappointed” as police investigate an alleged sexual assault involving several Swans players. Pavlich briefly fronted media in Sydney on Monday to address the alleged incident, which the club said took place in Melbourne on Sunday night. Loading “We’re still piecing together exactly what’s transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing. It’s safe to say that we’re extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation,” Pavlich said. “We understand the level of interest in the matter. There’s going to be lots of speculation, but given it’s a police matter right now, that is all that we can say.”



The Swans were staying at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne, near the MCG. They defeated Essendon by 36 points at the MCG earlier on Sunday evening. Police with clipboards and camera equipment were seen in the lobby of the hotel on Monday morning. By early afternoon there was no sign of Swans players or officials, and police appeared to have left the venue. The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Simon Schluter The Swans released a statement on Monday. “The Sydney Swans can confirm several players were involved in an alleged incident in Melbourne last night,” the club confirmed in a statement on Monday.



“The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage.” Pullman hotel staff would not comment. A witness said police at the venue had asked for CCTV footage, which covers public areas of the venue such as the lobby, stairs, lifts and floors. Victoria Police confirmed they were “investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne on August 17”.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour Hidden boardrooms, crime threats and nude pics: Inside the AFL’s most secretive unit “The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning,” it said in a statement. “The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing.” Swans board member and club great Michael O’Loughlin was spotted at Sydney’s domestic airport on Monday but declined to shed further light on the matter when approached for comment. “No, we’ll wait and see what the findings are, I don’t know,” O’Loughlin said.



The AFL confirmed the league had been notified by the Swans and said the matter rested with police. In cases such as this, the AFL’s integrity unit defers to police. More to come.

World.title: Haddara crime boss ‘lying in a pool of blood’ after suspected gangland ambush
World.content:
Gangland boss Fadi Haddara remains in a critical condition after being ambushed and shot in the face, stomach and chest outside his Altona North home. Haddara, 48, was found lying in a pool of blood by a family member next to his parked car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue, near Millers Road, before 8pm on Sunday. Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South Police said the attack was targeted, but they are keeping an open mind about the shooting’s connection to Melbourne’s tobacco war. Detective Inspector Adam Tilley, from the Victoria Police armed crime squad, confirmed Haddara had suffered “a number of” gunshot wounds to the upper body, and was receiving treatment in hospital.



“Shortly after 7.45pm, a family member of the victim attended a residence where they located the 48-year-old victim lying in a pool of blood next to his BMW,” Tilley said at a press conference. “We don’t have a suspect at this stage. We are going to keep an open mind. We’re going to review all the intelligence holdings that we have in relation to our victim. Everything is on the table, and everything will be fully explored.” Haddara was ambushed in his driveway on Sunday evening. Penny Stephens Neighbours, who did not want to be identified over fears of retaliation, said they heard multiple gunshots before 8pm. Police and paramedics were quickly on scene. The neighbours said they heard yelling inside the home as detectives arrived.



A family friend, who visited the scene on Monday morning, told reporters that Haddara was being treated in an intensive care unit with the bullets yet to be removed. He said there were children home when Haddara was shot. Haddara was accused of holding a commanding position over the illicit tobacco trade in Melbourne – which he has always denied – but was allegedly squeezed out by a new gangland boss, Kazem “Kaz” Hamad, in early 2024. Police were quickly on scene after the shooting. Nine Tilley said there were now concerns about a “flow-on effect” that could occur following the targeted attack, but that the armed crime squad was working with taskforces that target illicit tobacco syndicates. “Their intelligence holdings will be shared with us at the armed crime squad,” he said. “We’ve consulted with those agencies within Victoria Police, and we’ve consulted other agencies as well, law enforcement agencies.



“Ultimately, we’re worried about any flow-on effect that may occur and flow into the community, which is a concern to us.” Despite his reputation, neighbours said Haddara was friendly, often waving to neighbours as he drove along the street. Loading In a statement through their family lawyer, Zarah Garde-Wilson, the Haddara family requested privacy. “At this time, the family respectfully requests privacy as they focus on the wellbeing of their loved one. The family will not be providing comment at this time.”



The attempted hit came as a “shock”, underworld sources say. Haddara was a creature of habit, living and running many of his businesses in the same small pocket of Altona. Alleged gangland boss Fadi Haddara. “It’s where he grew up. (He stayed) probably because that’s what he knows,” a source said. Last year, as his hospitality empire crumbled, Fadi started a paint wholesaling business that was registered to the same address as the family’s Altona gym.



On Monday morning, half of Marigold Avenue remained completely blocked off. Police cars were seen parked outside the home and along the street. The road remained blocked off on Monday morning. Penny Stephens The front lights at Haddara’s home were on, but police tape blocked the driveway. The Age has previously reported allegations that Haddara surrendered his stake in the illicit tobacco smuggling and distribution market following a relentless firebombing and shooting campaign waged by Hamad in 2023-2024, including Fadi finding multiple GPS trackers on his car.

World.title: Dalaroo soil survey stretches WA copper-nickel target
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Dalaroo soil survey stretches WA copper-nickel target Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 17, 2026 — 1:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dalaroo Metals has expanded the footprint of its Watheroo copper-nickel-platinum group elements prospect in WA’s mid-north wheatbelt, with first-stage soil sampling extending a key copper anomaly by two square kilometres. The 106-sample program returned solid peak values of 284 parts per million (ppm) copper and 176ppm nickel, in addition to encouraging hits of up to 10 parts per billion for platinum, palladium and gold. Quartz outcrop at Dalaroo Metals’ Watheroo copper-nickel- PGE project in Western Australia. The fresh results extend the copper-in-soil geochemical response south of a historical sampling area, with the area enclosed by the 40ppm copper contour now covering two square kilometres. Dalaroo says the multi-element soil results shows a strong spatial association with both mapped mafic-ultramafic rocks and a significant underlying magnetic feature, strengthening its interpretation of a large-scale intrusive system. The company is pursuing a Julimar-style magmatic sulphide exploration model at Watheroo, which is centred on an impressive 7-km by 3km magnetic anomaly.



‘Peak results of 284ppm copper and 176ppm nickel are encouraging.’ Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan The project sits on the western margin of the Yilgarn Craton, a geological setting that was thrust into the spotlight following Chalice Mining’s world-class Gonneville nickel-copper-PGE discovery at its Julimar project 90km to the south. That discovery sparked a land rush along the craton margin, a region previously overlooked due to significant surface cover. Dalaroo’s work at Watheroo is a textbook case of building a geological story from the ground up. The company has layered historical data with its own more recent magnetic surveys and is now overlaying that with surface geochemistry. The latest results look to have firmed up the eastern contact of the buried mafic-ultramafic intrusion as a priority hunting ground for potential sulphide accumulation. Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan said: “Stage 1 has extended the Watheroo copper and nickel soil response south of the historical sampling area. Peak results of 284 ppm copper and 176 ppm nickel are encouraging and, together with the broader multi-element response, provide a clear focus for follow-up work.” Whilst Watheroo is shaping up as a key local asset, Dalaroo is also advancing a diverse portfolio of projects across multiple jurisdictions. In Côte d’Ivoire, the company has cleared the final hurdles for a major maiden drilling campaign at its Bondoukou Gold Ridge project. Following a recent $2.5 million capital raise, Dalaroo has expanded its planned reverse circulation drilling program to 12,000m from 10,000m to systematically test three priority gold targets along a 7km-long anomalous trend with drilling set to kick off any day.



Further afield in southern Greenland, Dalaroo recently wrapped up the largest-ever field program at its Blue Lagoon rare earths project. The company says the work has already upgraded the project from an early-stage concept into a well-defined regional rare earths system with four new prospects identified. More than 200 samples from that program are in the lab with a steady stream of news flow expected. Adding another string to its bow back in Western Australia, Dalaroo also holds the Lyons River project in the Gascoyne province where it was awarded a government co-funding grant for drilling after confirming the discovery of a gold system there in April. The company is not resting on its laurels at Watheroo, with plans already underway for the next phase of work. A further 360 soil samples are planned for collection to extend the geochemical coverage northwards and to provide closer-spaced infill sampling over priority areas. The infill work will tighten the grid to a nominal 100m line spacing by 50m sample spacing. Following the comprehensive soil program, Dalaroo plans to undertake ground-based induced polarisation geophysics to hunt for chargeable anomalies at depth that could represent disseminated sulphides. The combined datasets will then be used to rank and define potential targets for a maiden drilling campaign. While the latest results from Watheroo build a compelling case for a Julimar-style prize in WA, Dalaroo is clearly not a one-trick pony. As the rods start to turn in West Africa, a pipeline of rare earths news from Greenland and multiple irons in the fire back home, the company is methodically assembling a diverse portfolio of exploration opportunities, with the hunt for WA’s next big nickel-copper-PGE prize just one chapter in a much larger story. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Nashville star Hayden Panettiere dies at age 36
World.content:
Updated CultureCelebrityVale Nashville star Hayden Panettiere dies at age 36 Nell Geraets August 17, 2026 — 1:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hayden Panettiere, an American actor best known for her roles in TV shows Heroes and Nashville, has died at age 36. Panettiere’s father, Skip Panettiere, confirmed her death in a statement to several US news outlets on Monday. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden,” he said. “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.” Hayden Panettiere in 2022. Getty Her father also asked for privacy as his family “takes time to process this unimaginable loss”. Further details about her death, including the cause, are unknown. Panettiere’s publicist, Kasey Kitchen, told NBC News that her death was being investigated; however, it remained unclear whether she was referring to a coronial investigation into her death or an autopsy.



“There’s an investigation ongoing,” Kitchen said. “We should know more tomorrow.” Panettiere began her career at the age of four, joining the soap opera One Life to Live as Sarah Roberts. She went on to star in several television series and films, though she was best recognised as Claire Bennet in the popular sci-fi series Heroes, and as Juliette Barnes in Nashville. Panettiere as Claire Bennet in Heroes. NBC/Michael Muller Beyond those two series, she also starred in Raising Helen, Remember the Titans, Ice Princess, I Love You Beth Cooper and Scream 4. Earlier this year, the actor released a memoir titled This Is Me: A Reckoning. In it, she recounted the impact of being a child actor, her past alcohol addiction and giving up custody of her daughter.



Panettiere had one child, Kaya Evdokia Klitschko, in 2014 with her now ex-fiance Wladimir Klitschko, a Ukrainian former professional boxer. Speaking on the Jay Shetty Podcast in May, the actor said she did not react well when Klitschko told her their daughter would live with him in Europe permanently. “I was struggling with mental health and anxiety and the postpartum and having to act my way through it, and just feeling like I completely lost myself,” she said. “I think a misconception is that I have been in the past forced into treatment when, in fact, I have been the one who sought it out – who was saying I desperately need help.” Panettiere with her daughter Kaya. ninevms She had fallen into a “horrible cycle” of depression, anxiety, alcoholism and substance abuse, she told the British podcaster, all in an attempt to “find her way out of the darkness”.



Panettiere entered an in-patient treatment centre in early 2020 where she worked on overcoming her opioid and alcohol addiction. She detailed her addiction and sobriety in a 2022 interview with People magazine. “With the opiates and alcohol I was doing anything to make me feel happy for a moment,” she told the magazine. “Then I’d feel worse than I did before. I was in a cycle of self-destruction. “[Now] it’s an everyday choice, and I’m checking in with myself all the time … But I’m just so grateful to be part of this world again, and I will never take it for granted again.” More to come Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Like a living hell’: Rapist Ralph Carr unrecognisable in court appearance
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts ‘Like a living hell’: Rapist Ralph Carr unrecognisable in court appearance Erin Pearson August 17, 2026 — 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Convicted rapist Ralph Carr has described his life as “a living hell” after the former talent manager was found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman more than 30 years his junior. In a pre-sentencing hearing on Monday at the County Court of Victoria, the 66-year-old appeared without his recognisable black wig and tailored suits, instead sporting a shaved head and grey prison-issued tracksuit. Ralph Carr and his connections. Aresna Villanueva The court heard Carr was confined to his prison cell for 23 hours a day, and believes the verdict has “destroyed” his career. Psychiatric assessments presented to the court on Monday painted a picture of a troubled man with poor mental health, which largely coincided with the legal proceedings and his concerns about being publicly named in connection to the rape case.



“It’s like a living hell,” Carr told a psychiatrist. Related Article Courts Melbourne’s worst-kept secret: Behind the celebrity trappings, Ralph Carr was known simply as ‘The Rug’ Defence barrister Dermot Dann, KC, said that after the suppression order over Carr’s identity was lifted and he was publicly named, the risks to his mental health became “so much more dire”, with his risk of self-harm elevated by his perceived damage to his reputation and identity. Dann told the court Carr was experiencing “profound shame” and “nightmares” since being jailed. “Twenty-three hours a day [in a prison cell] is likely to have an adverse impact on his mental health,” the barrister said. Thirteen character references, including a number from family members, were tendered to the court.



As Carr stood in the dock at the back of the courtroom, an older woman in the front row of the courtroom blew him a kiss before approaching and saying, “Love to you lots.” The high-profile sport and entertainment manager, who once counted Brownlow medallist Dustin Martin as a client and business partner and singer Tina Arena as his ex-wife, was last month found guilty of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault following a jury trial in the County Court. Dustin Martin poses with Carr, then the footballer’s manager, after winning the 2017 Brownlow Medal. Getty Images Carr maintains his innocence and has flagged the intention to seek a stay of the sentence, arguing the jury got it wrong. The jury heard the victim, then aged in her 20s, had spoken with Carr over potentially working with him and recalled being invited to his “larger than life” converted warehouse complete with a sauna, extensive wine collection, a glass office and a grand piano.



Carr – whose company, Ralph Carr Management, called itself one of the most successful and respected artist management companies in Australia – suggested the woman could help him work on his pending autobiography and film script. Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted The jury heard that after consuming alcohol and cocaine together one night in 2023, Carr began consoling the victim over a broken relationship and then raped her. “He kept coming back. Putting his hands all over me. He didn’t care that I was crying,” she told police. The woman called her mother about what had happened, and the mother immediately phoned police, the trial heard. The victim stayed at the address, but said she locked herself in another room until police arrived about 3.45am.



The jury found Carr guilty on all charges following three days of deliberations. Dann, the defence barrister, told the trial the victim was an unreliable witness who had a financial motive to lie. He compared the woman to a fiction writer. Carr (left) with Tina Arena in 1993. Rodger Cummins The prosecution conceded there were inconsistencies in the victim’s evidence, but maintained she spoke truthfully about the night in question. During the trial, Carr called in longtime friends in the legal and entertainment business to give character evidence on his behalf, including barrister friend Marcus Clarke, KC, and entertainment industry consultant Adrian David Marchesani, who gave character evidence.



His identity was suppressed for three years after his legal team obtained, in March 2023, a secrecy order to conceal his alleged involvement in the assault on the woman, citing mental health concerns for their client if he was publicly named. The order prevented the media from naming Carr, reporting his age and the industry he worked in, and from publishing pixelated photographs. Carr outside court in July during his trial. Luis Enrique Ascui The West Melbourne man was born to immigrant parents in Melbourne, and raised in Fitzroy North. After completing year 12, he began working in a factory making washers to earn money for his family, and then worked in a supermarket and the insurance industry.



From there, his interest in music eventually led to him setting up his management company. Dann said that throughout Carr’s 35 years in the industry he initially managed musicians and bands and then branched out to sporting personalities. “He was very devoted to his work and his clients. His work meant a lot to him,” Dann said. The hearing continues. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination of ‘complainant C’  begins after court told Jones offered man tour of Packer suite before kissing him in walk-in wardrobe
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day nine of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleague Clare Sibthorpe will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear further evidence today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Monday. KATE GERAGHTY

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Jones is charged with indecently assaulting “C” eight times over a five-month period by touching and kissing him without his consent.

“C” told the court on Friday that Jones bombarded him with “love-bombing” in text messages before the alleged incidents started.

He said he told Jones “no” repeatedly before the then 2GB host kissed him for the first time in the lift of the broadcaster’s harbourside apartment, but the “extraordinary” power imbalance stopped him speaking out as the alleged assaults continued.

He also told the court that Jones touched him under the table on the penis over his clothing at a lunch in Sydney in front of other guests. He said one guest asked him after the lunch if he had “copped a feel”, a remark that left him “deeply embarrassed”.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

The move comes against a backdrop of feverish activity in the Australian gold sector. The buoyant market is keeping mining service providers busy, with contractors being locked in across the state as producers look to capitalise on the high-price environment.

MEGA Resources’ fleet of Cat 777 dump trucks may soon see service on Forrestania Resources Tycho open pit mining operation in WA.

The deal also includes a staged payment profile with some deferred arrangements in the early months, in a savvy commercial move that should help manage cash flow as operations ramp up.
